outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Controllable Text-to-Image Generation
outline.description: Over the past few years, the field of artificial intelligence has witnessed a paradigm shift driven by large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Systems such as Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2, and Imagen have demonstrated an unprecedented ability to synthesize high-fidelity, photorealistic images from natural language descriptions. These models operate by learning a complex mapping between textual embeddings and visual representations, effectively internalizing vast amounts of world knowledge regarding objects, styles, lighting conditions, and artistic techniques. For instance, Stable Diffusion leverages a latent space constructed by a variational autoencoder (VQ-GAN), allowing it to generate images efficiently in a compressed representation before decoding them back to pixels. outline.description: To appreciate the novelty and efficacy of Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), one must first step back from the mechanics of gradient descent and examine the geometric nature of neural representations themselves. Large text-to-image diffusion models possess immense generative capabilities, yet adapting them to specific downstream tasks without degrading their pre-trained semantic abilities presents a profound challenge. Traditional finetuning strategies rely heavily on heuristic assumptions about model proximity, often assuming that keeping the updated weights close to the original weights in Euclidean space is sufficient to preserve knowledge. outline.description: To understand the necessity of Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT), one must first grasp the fundamental mechanism by which neural networks encode semantic information. Traditional intuitions suggest that the magnitude of neuron activations carries significant weight in determining outputs. However, recent theoretical and empirical observations indicate that angular relationships between neurons—specifically their directions on a unit hypersphere—are far more critical for preserving semantic content than their magnitudes.
